newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM to dissolve parliament ready for election.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM to dissolve parliament ready for election.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto will dissolve Japan's parliament on Friday, his political allies said on Thursday, the first formal step towards calling early general elections expected on October 20.
The polls, eight months earlier than needed, are timed to take advantage of an improving economy and to come well before a rise in an unpopular sales tax scheduled for next April.

Political commentators say there are few other pressing issues for Hashimoto at present, offering him a chance to defend his record in office and push his campaign to reduce the stifling bureaucracy blamed for a host of Japan's woes.

Hashimoto had strongly favoured an autumn election but was held up by resistance from the other two parties in his ruling coalition. The two smaller parties are expected to lose seats in the election, which would be for the Lower House of parliament, because of a change in the electoral system.
Word of the plan to dissolve the Lower House came from Shoichi Ide, president of the Sakigake party, after a meeting of coalition leaders.
"The prime minister told us that there was no other time when parliament could be dissolved than the opening of its special session on Friday," Ide told reporters.
He did not give a date, but government officials have said openly that a vote is expected on October 20. The polls must be called within 40 days of a dissolution of parliament.
Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) is expected to get the most votes in the election but no single party is likely to capture a majority in the 500-seat Lower House.
This means the LDP would be forced to form a another coalition with one or more of its political rivals.
The main opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) is projected to finish second with around 200 Lower House seats.
Except for the planned rise in the sales tax to five percent from three percent, there are few major policy issues facing the country.

Japan's economy is recovering from a slump that followed the bursting of a "bubble" of soaring asset prices in the early 1990s. But analysts and government experts agree it remains fragile and could be seriously set back by a rise in the sales tax.
Hashimoto is Japan's fourth prime minister since the last general election in 1993, when the pro-business LDP lost its grip on power for the first time in 38 years.
The polls will be the first under a system designed to make campaigning less costly and reduce dependence on political donations.
In the new system, enacted in 1994, candidates will contest 300 seats in single-seat constituencies, with the other 200 seats decided through proportional representation.
Members of the less-powerful Upper House are elected on a fixed schedule unrelated to the terms of the Lower House.
